planting.note: Root semi-hardwood nodal cuttings in warm, humid conditions and transplant outdoors only after nighttime temperatures stay reliably above 60F.

directions: Matico is a fast-growing, multi-stemmed Amazonian shrub whose crushed leaves have long been applied topically as a folk wound dressing and brewed as a digestive tea. Propagate from nodal stem cuttings, which root readily in moist, humus-rich media, since seed is rarely available commercially. Site in bright, filtered light under taller canopy in humid, frost-free gardens, and keep soil consistently moist but well drained. Once established the shrub tolerates brief dry spells and can be cut back hard to encourage bushy new growth for repeated leaf harvest.
sources: Kew Royal Botanic Gardens - Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Start seed indoors in warm, humid conditions and transplant outside once nights stay above 60F, giving the scrambling vine a trellis or host shrub to climb.

directions: Suma is a vigorous, climbing perennial from the Amazon basin grown for its deep, sweet-tasting root, prized in traditional medicine as a general tonic and adaptogen thanks to its saponin and ecdysteroid content. It thrives in rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil under the dappled light of a humid tropical or subtropical garden, scrambling over neighboring shrubs or a trellis as it matures. Roots are left undisturbed for several growing seasons to bulk up before harvest, similar in patience required to true ginseng. Protect from any frost and mulch heavily to keep the root zone consistently warm and moist through the growing season.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plant Products

planting.note: Direct sow fresh seed in fall before the ground freezes, or in very early spring, into loose, deep, sandy loam that encourages a long, straight taproot.

directions: Fang Feng is a cold-hardy, drought-tolerant Apiaceae grown in northern China for its aromatic taproot, a staple ingredient in traditional Chinese medicine for centuries. It produces finely divided, carrot-like foliage and flat umbels of small white flowers typical of the carrot family, followed by ribbed seed that loses viability quickly and should be sown fresh. Deep, loose, unobstructed soil is essential for straight root development, and the plant resents heavy clay, waterlogging, or salty soils. Roots are traditionally dug in the second year of growth after the foliage has died back, then dried for storage.
sources: ATTRA Sustainable Agriculture (National Center for Appropriate Technology)

planting.note: Sow fresh seed immediately after harvest, as viability drops within days, and provide a sturdy trellis for this vigorous climbing liana once transplanted outdoors.

directions: Guarana is an Amazonian climbing shrub cultivated in Brazil for its seed capsules, which contain a notably high concentration of caffeine and are roasted and ground into a traditional stimulant paste. It tolerates poor, acidic, aluminum-rich soils in its native range but requires consistent warmth, high humidity, and a strong support structure to climb as it matures. Seed must be started fresh because it loses viability within days of ripening, and germination itself can take several months. Once established, expect years of vegetative growth before the vine produces its first clusters of red, seed-bearing capsules.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plant Products
Kew Royal Botanic Gardens - Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Root leafless hardwood cuttings with rooting hormone in a sandy, fast-draining nursery mix, and transplant only after a full growing season once frost danger has passed for good.

directions: Guggul is a slow-growing, thorny, drought-adapted shrub of the arid scrublands of Rajasthan and Gujarat, tapped for the fragrant oleo-gum-resin exuded from its bark, a resin central to Ayurvedic medicine for millennia. Because seed germination is slow and unreliable, most growers propagate it from hardwood stem cuttings rooted under warm, dry nursery conditions. It demands intense heat, full sun, and gritty, sharply draining soil, and will not tolerate frost, prolonged wet feet, or humid climates. Wild populations are now conservation-threatened from overharvesting, so cultivated stock is preferred wherever it can be sourced.
sources: Kew Royal Botanic Gardens - Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Scarify the hard seed coat and soak before sowing to improve germination, then transplant near a trellis or host shrub once temperatures are reliably warm and frost-free.

directions: Vidanga is a sprawling, woody, scandent shrub native to the forest margins of India's Western Ghats, valued in Ayurvedic tradition for its small peppercorn-like berries. Its hard seed coat is dormant and benefits from mechanical scarification before sowing to achieve reliable germination. In cultivation it needs a host tree, fence, or trellis to scramble over as it matures, along with dappled light and consistently moist, well-drained soil typical of a humid subtropical or tropical understory. Berries are harvested once fully ripe and dried for use in traditional preparations, though overharvesting from the wild has made cultivated sources increasingly important.
sources: Kew Royal Botanic Gardens - Plants of the World Online
